Here’s a detector-cell contract you can hand to a coder or hardware designer.

# Detector-cell implementation contract

## Purpose

Implement one branch detector cell that converts branch absorbed power into a **rare discrete nucleation event**, with:

$$
\lambda \approx \alpha,P_{\text{abs}}
$$

over the calibrated operating range, followed by a latch-compatible output.

This cell is for the **pre-click detector layer** only. It does not compute branch weights; it only converts local branch intensity into a stochastic first-trigger process.

---

## 1. Functional role

Each detector cell sits on one analyzer/readout branch.

### Input

* branch voltage/current or equivalent absorbed-power signal
* bias supply for metastable/avalanche operation
* reset signal from global controller

### Output

* binary nucleation pulse
* latched “winner request” line to common closure block
* optional analog monitor lines for diagnostics

### Required behavior

* no deterministic threshold crossing under normal operating conditions
* rare stochastic trigger events
* trigger rate approximately proportional to absorbed branch power
* once triggered, emit a clean digital pulse suitable for common-mode latch logic

---

## 2. Operating-point specification

The detector must be biased in a **rare-event metastable regime**.

### Required operating regime

At zero or negligible branch power:

* spontaneous trigger rate is low but nonzero
* cell remains stable for long periods
* no self-oscillation
* no deterministic switching

At nominal branch power:

* trigger events occur stochastically
* trigger hazard increases approximately linearly with absorbed power
* output pulse amplitude and timing are well-defined

### Bias target

Choose a bias point (B_0) such that:

* below bias: trigger rate too small to measure in practical time
* above bias: cell self-fires or becomes strongly nonlinear
* at (B_0): rare-event regime with usable dynamic range

### Engineering acceptance

For calibrated input powers (P\in[P_{\min},P_{\max}]),
$$
\lambda(P)\approx \lambda_0+\alpha P
$$
with small residual nonlinearity over the intended range.

---

## 3. Rate-vs-power calibration

This is the most important requirement.

### Target law

For one detector branch:
$$
\lambda(P_{\text{abs}})=\lambda_{\text{dark}}+\alpha P_{\text{abs}} + \varepsilon(P)
$$
where:

* (\lambda_{\text{dark}}) is dark-count rate
* (\alpha) is branch gain
* (\varepsilon(P)) is calibration error

### Required linearity

Over the operating range:
$$
\frac{|\varepsilon(P)|}{\lambda_{\text{dark}}+\alpha P} < \delta_{\text{lin}}
$$

Recommended first target:

* (\delta_{\text{lin}} \le 5%)

Stretch target:

* (\delta_{\text{lin}} \le 2%)

### Calibration procedure

For each cell:

1. drive the branch with a calibrated matched source
2. measure absorbed power (P_{\text{abs}})
3. record trigger counts over fixed windows
4. fit (\lambda(P))
5. extract:

   * (\lambda_{\text{dark}})
   * (\alpha)
   * linearity error

### Deliverable

A fitted calibration curve and residual plot for each detector cell.

---

## 4. Dark counts

Dark counts are unavoidable and must be characterized.

### Definition

$$
\lambda_{\text{dark}} = \lambda(P_{\text{abs}}=0)
$$

### Requirement

Dark counts must be:

* low compared with nominal signal-trigger rates
* stable in time
* similar across matched branches

### Acceptance target

For nominal branch power (P_{\text{nom}}),
$$
\lambda_{\text{dark}} \ll \alpha P_{\text{nom}}
$$

Recommended first target:
$$
\lambda_{\text{dark}} \le 0.01, \alpha P_{\text{nom}}
$$

### Measurement

* collect long no-signal runs
* estimate mean dark rate and variance
* verify no bursty pathological behavior

---

## 5. Matching tolerance across branches

Born-like competition depends critically on matched detector cells.

### Parameters that must match

Across all four joint branches:

* dark count rate (\lambda_{\text{dark}})
* power-to-hazard gain (\alpha)
* pulse amplitude
* pulse width
* latency distribution
* reset recovery time

### Required matching

For cells (i,j),
$$
\left|\frac{\alpha_i-\alpha_j}{\bar\alpha}\right| < \delta_\alpha
$$
and
$$
\left|\frac{\lambda_{\text{dark},i}-\lambda_{\text{dark},j}}{\bar\lambda_{\text{dark}}+\lambda_*}\right| < \delta_d
$$

where (\lambda_*) is a stabilizing reference scale to avoid meaningless blow-up when dark rates are tiny.

Recommended first targets:

* (\delta_\alpha \le 2%)
* pulse-width mismatch (\le 5%)
* mean latency mismatch (\le 5%)

### Why this matters

If branch gains differ, outcome probabilities become
$$
P_i \propto \alpha_i w_i
$$
instead of pure (w_i).

So gain matching is a physics requirement, not just an engineering nicety.

---

## 6. Latch output interface

The detector cell must hand off to the global closure block cleanly.

### Output signal

Each cell outputs a binary pulse:

* rising edge = nucleation event
* pulse width fixed or stretched enough for reliable capture

### Interface requirements

* logic-compatible output level
* monotonic rising edge
* no double pulses per event
* optional local latch flag

### Timing requirements

Let (t_{\text{nuc}}) be the nucleation time and (t_{\text{out}}) the digital edge time.

Define detector latency:
$$
\tau_{\text{lat}} = t_{\text{out}}-t_{\text{nuc}}
$$

Requirement:

* latency jitter small relative to inter-branch competition timescale
* output pulse generated fast enough that common closure can suppress losers before substantial rival growth

Recommended target:

* (\tau_{\text{lat}}) and jitter both much smaller than the common latch settling time

### Reset behavior

After global reset:

* cell returns to metastable operating point
* no retained winner memory
* no elevated retrigger probability beyond specified dead time

---

## 7. Dead time and recovery

### Definition

After a click, the detector may be insensitive for some recovery interval (T_{\text{dead}}).

### Requirement

* dead time must be well defined
* recovery to calibrated (\lambda(P)) must be repeatable
* no branch-dependent long-tail memory effects

### Acceptance

Measure repeated click/reset cycles and verify:

* stable recovery time
* no drift in (\alpha)
* no drift in dark count rate

---

## 8. Standalone validation tests

Before integrating with the shared-core model, each detector cell must pass:

### Test A — dark-count characterization

No signal input, measure (\lambda_{\text{dark}})

### Test B — rate-vs-power sweep

Matched absorbed-power injections, fit (\lambda(P))

### Test C — pulse quality

Verify one clean digital output per trigger

### Test D — reset/recovery

Repeated click-reset cycles

### Test E — branch matching

Compare all fabricated cells under identical drive

---

## 9. Integration-level validation

Once connected to the branch-weight generator:

### Integration target

If branch absorbed powers satisfy
$$
P_i(t)=\Gamma(t)w_i
$$
with common envelope (\Gamma(t)), then measured hazard rates should satisfy
$$
\lambda_i(t)\approx \lambda_{\text{dark}}+\alpha \Gamma(t) w_i
$$

### Desired competition law

Ignoring dark counts and mismatch,
$$
P(\text{branch }i\text{ wins}) \approx w_i
$$

### What to monitor

* winner frequencies vs target weights
* distortion from dark counts
* distortion from gain mismatch
* distortion from latency mismatch

---

## 10. Minimal mathematical spec

For branch (i), the detector cell should approximate:

$$
\lambda_i(t)=\lambda_{\text{dark},i}+\alpha_i P_i(t)
$$

with:

* (\alpha_i \approx \alpha)
* (\lambda_{\text{dark},i} \approx \lambda_{\text{dark}})

and output a digital nucleation pulse at the first realized event time.

That is the entire detector-layer contract in one line.

---

# Deliverables

For each detector-cell design candidate, require:

1. schematic
2. operating-point bias values
3. simulated or measured (\lambda(P)) curve
4. dark-count characterization
5. pulse timing/shape characterization
6. reset/dead-time characterization
7. branch-to-branch matching summary
